title: Representation-Dependent Machine Learning of the Isotropic-Nematic Transition in the Lebwohl-Lasher Model
authors: Maninder Kaur, Aojie Xue, David P Landau
abstract: Machine-learning detection of phase transitions depends not only on the learning algorithm, but also on whether the input representation preserves the symmetries of the system. We examine this for the weak first-order isotropic--nematic transition of the three-dimensional Lebwohl--Lasher model, whose apolar and continuously degenerate nematic phase makes raw molecular configurations a challenging input for unsupervised learning. Principal component analysis (PCA) and a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) fail to identify the transition from raw configurations because rotationally equivalent nematic states can appear far apart in the input space. When the same configurations are transformed into a rotationally invariant local-correlation representation, both methods recover transition-sensitive signatures and bimodal coexistence distributions. A supervised three-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN), by contrast, accurately predicts the scalar order parameter from raw configurations when given order-parameter labels. The Lebwohl-Lasher model therefore separates unsupervised phase discovery from supervised order-parameter regression and shows that symmetry-respecting input representations are needed for unsupervised machine learning in orientationally ordered systems.
summary: This paper uses machine learning to study the isotropic-nematic phase transition in the Lebwohl-Lasher model. It demonstrates that unsupervised methods fail if raw molecular data are used because global rotational symmetries obscure the physical signal. However, by transforming the input into a rotationally invariant representation, the ML techniques successfully recover clear signatures of the phase transition.
main_problem: The study investigates whether machine learning detection of phase transitions depends critically on whether the input representation preserves the underlying symmetries of the physical system.
main_result: Unsupervised ML methods (PCA, CAE) fail to detect the transition using raw molecular configurations but successfully recover transition signatures when the input is transformed into a rotationally invariant local-correlation representation.
method: The authors compare unsupervised learning techniques (PCA and CAE) against supervised regression (CNN) applied to data from Monte Carlo simulations of the Lebwohl-Lasher model.
model_or_system: The system studied is the three-dimensional Lebwohl-Lasher (LL) model, which models nematic liquid crystals exhibiting a weak first-order isotropic--nematic phase transition. The Hamiltonian interaction is apolar and possesses continuous rotational degeneracy.
key_observables: Scalar nematic order parameter ($S$), bimodal coexistence distributions, leading PCA scores, and CAE latent coordinates.
important_parameters: Lattice sizes ($L=50, 60, 80$) and the coupling constant ratio $J/k_B T = 1$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption tested is that for unsupervised ML to work on systems with continuous symmetries, the input representation must be invariant under those symmetry transformations.
figures_summary: Figures compare thermodynamic benchmarks ($\langle S angle$ vs $T$, $P(S)$) against results from PCA/CAE using raw data (showing failure) versus bond-$P_2$ data (showing success), alongside CNN regression plots.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and transition, then systematically tests ML methods: first on raw configurations (failure), followed by symmetry-adapted representations (success for unsupervised learning), concluding with a comparison to supervised prediction accuracy.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the core methodological lesson—that input representation must respect underlying symmetries for feature extraction—is highly relevant when designing quantum state representations or observables for ML analysis in AMO physics.
